#6762. With the ‘New’ Yeezy, Ye Says He Wants to ‘Let the Clothes Do the Talking.’ But Who’s Listening?

“I don’t have a lot of words tonight,” Ye told me, not long after concluding his Yeezy Season 01 runway show in Los Angeles on Wednesday evening. “I’ll let the clothes do the talking.”

You might read that quote and be surprised to hear that Ye said it warmly, with an all-32-bared smile. But for those still paying attention, his relatively upbeat demeanor tracks with the tame-not-turnt persona that Ye has performed through most of 2026; the one that’s been slowly-but-surely trying to reamass the cultural capital he’s spent most of the last decade either annihilating or reclaiming. Legions of fans have proven they’re still all in; the culture at large remains justifiably dubious. The question this week is, how will Ye’s return to fashion affect the calculus?

Upon arrival, a typical Hollywood warehouse exterior turned into a Frank Herbert-esque interior as soon as you crossed the threshold. Inside, a hundred or so guests sat on two rows of unbroken benches that encircled a large white mound in the center, lit by a heavenly white glow from above. Inside was a mix of the usual cool kids: models (including the runway-favorite teen rapper Nettspend) and recurring characters in the overarching, enduring Kanye Universe. There was Fear of God founder Jerry Lorenzo, who made conversation with Don C, while 2 Chainz was patiently posted up in a hooded black leather coat like ’98 Wesley Snipes. Big Sean, rebuffing the sweltering indoor temperatures in a shearling jacket over a crewneck sweater, caught up with Hit-Boy.

Models on the Yeezy Season 01 runway, which featured a characteristically minimalist set piece.

The 19-year-old rapper Nettspend walked in the show.

Once everyone was seated, the lights dimmed as the unmistakable opening piano note of “Runaway” set the show into motion, with one lone model striding out in a killer black trench. From there, two more models, men this time, walked out in the opposite direction; what followed was a bit of organized chaos with the number of models and paths alternating at random intervals to the tune of a playlist that zipped between new Ye music (UK garage vibes, it would seem) and a gothic orchestra not unlike the scores Danny Elfman used to chef up for Tim Burton.

The fits were crisp, practical and tactical. Most of the menswear was ready-made for basic maneuvers, while the women’s looks were sleek and casual, with a few Milla Jovovich-in-Fifth-Element skimpy ensembles thrown in because Ye can only restrain himself but so much. The most notable thing, about the guys especially, were the relatively streamlined silhouettes: close-cropped coats, bombers and vests, fitted pants and sweats. Where past Ye lines championed and emblazoned the path for the baggy wave, with oversized boots and pants you could swim in, Ye seemed to be brazenly planting a flag back on the opposite end of the spectrum.

Nearly 12 years, and a dozen lifetimes, since his debut Yeezy Season 1 runway show in 2015, the notion of a “Season 01”—his first formal showing since his damning 2022 show in Paris, the one with the “White Lives Matter” shirts—is a conspicuous attempt to clear the slate. All of his previous shows had been produced in collaboration with Adidas, who severed ties with Ye four years ago, after he tweeted a tirade of antisemetic remarks. This time around, to let the clothes tell it, Ye is locked in. I don’t have an image of every single Yeezy Season line seared into my brain, but I feel comfortable saying Ye’s latest was the first time I looked at one of his collections and objectively thought, I could wear that. Most of the gear is quite solid—and familiar Ye's running the same playbook with Season 01 that he’s run with his music, and to some degree, his persona. It’s the Yeezy gear you know and love(d), refined to make it that much more palatable, similar to the way a song like “Whatever Works” puts him back over chipmunk’d soul samples. And true to the title, it does indeed; the fact that it does is maybe a testament to the brilliance that got lost in the insanity. But is playing the hits (quite literally, with “Runaway” opening the show) what we want from one of the most paradigm-shifting—and absolutely chaotic—creative minds of our time?

Historically, Ye’s designs are so focused on an idea of utilitarianism that they ultimately come off as a bit drab, if not downright dystopian. Essentials like hoodies and beefy leather jackets are still central to his vision, but as the models strode around in his usual earth-toned palette—save for a handful of black looks to start, and a bright pop of reds at the end—it became clear that Ye was putting on the same show in a different kind of stadium. The same sci-fi silhouettes, tweaked to their cleanest shape and most pleasing hue, sans screenprinted hate speech. Ideologically, the runway show wasn’t far off from the experience of hearing his 2007 hit “Good Life” all these years later, ringing off stadium speakers, carrying 80,000 people along on a wave of wistfulness— even if Ye himself only performed approximately 75% of the lyrics against a backing track.

In keeping with all of his other moves this year, Yeezy Season 01 is Ye presenting a safer, rule-abiding version of himself: Ye with just art, no antics. Much in the way that his latest album, Bully, eschewed any lyrics that say, shouted out R. Kelly or Bill Cosby (which is more than can be said about 2024’s Vultures 1), it felt like a deep sigh of relief to see him present clothes that don’t feature appalling slogans, at a fashion show with Candace Owens nowhere in sight. But the compromise for a sanitized Kanye is also one that can’t help but feel anodyne as well. The New Ye doesn’t needle, but he’s lost Old Ye’s knack for trying something new. Of course, we’re also well over a decade into the Yeezy experiment—at this point, the present has caught up to the futuristic vision Ye first dreamt up back in 2015. There’s a whole new generation of aspiring designers creating in his image, kids who fancy themselves trailblazers whose paths just loop back to Ye: streamer Kai Cenat just launched his own clothing brand, Vivet, while N3on attended Wednesday night’s show, skipping the Yeezy space gleefully documenting every interaction. It feels as though all of this has happened before, and all of it will happen again.

Mystery. Intrigue. Chaos. This is the typical life cycle for a Ye project, be it music, fashion, or otherwise. An announcement materializes, hype ensues. Then, inevitably, the seams start to show and it becomes apparent that he isn’t inviting you on a pre-planned journey so much as building the plane in real time, seconds before takeoff. And then, through sheer force of will, or maybe even genius, the result ends up so captivating that the speedbumps hardly matter. He’s still a master showman, and all it takes is a strong yearning for the Old Ye to find yourself surrendering to it. The efficacy of that last factor, though, has undeniably waned over the years. For much of the 2020s, in the midst of many a manic outburst or worse, Ye’s messes have hardly cohered into something objectively beautiful. The intrigue curdled into perverse bemusement; for every unwavering diehard fan, there was a rubbernecker tapped in to watch the circus.

The 2026 version of Ye has been an exercise in proving how many people will show up when he shuts up, and whether he can make it back from the brink if he delivers the right spectacle.

The result is the most well-oiled the Yeezy Machine has ever been. An album that more or less dropped when he said it would, for once. A smattering of live shows across the world, each in a sold-out stadium boasting record-breaking rap concert attendance where he leans on his most enduring strengths: visual spectacle and a bulletproof catalog. The only area left to renegotiate is fashion…which brings us back to Wednesday night in LA.

These are the scenes you’d expect at a Ye event, but the first sign that the overall vibe was different and more relaxed was that the man himself was at the door, tucked off into a hallway, immaculately dressed in a fitted all-black leather fit offset by a ridiculously large and ornate gold waist fixture—every bit the Dune-caliber fit as the space we were standing in required. Ahead of the show, he posed backstage flanked by his wife, Bianca Censori, and the four kids he shares with his ex, Kim Kardashian (including 13-year-old North, who was sporting her unmistakable blue-raspberry locks). At Yeezy events past, you’d expect to see harried staff scrambling, while Ye was somewhere out of sight but exuding stress and anxiety out into the atmosphere. But on Wednesday, the 49-year-old beamed as friends made their way past him to their seats. Even a three-piece-suited Kid Cudi came over to say hello.

Ye backstage with his children, from left: North, Psalm, Chicago, and Saint West.

Fifteen years ago, Yeezy Season 01 would’ve caused a massive sea change in the menswear world almost instantaneously, with the wave starting in SoHo then slowly emanating out into the beyond. In 2026, does Kanye still move that needle? The Year in Ye has been one big display of his ability to Don Draper the culture at large, and shock us all by “how much it never happened.” There’s no controversy big enough to keep him away for too long and very few fences he can’t mend.

For example, Sean and Cudi ceased their umpteenth falling out with their old label boss two months ago at a guest-packed, blockbuster homecoming show in Chicago on Ye’s tour stop; their show of support tonight only underlined how deeply the hatchet has been buried yet again. When I spoke to Big Sean after the show, he could only marvel at how much Ye has “given” to the culture across all different categories. One-time GOOD Music COO Steven Victor said the show made him feel like Ye “has his shit together,” noting that Ye admitted to him that he was still working out the model patterns hours before showtime. In past Yeezy Seasons, the cram-effect would’ve been apparent, but here, Victor said he wouldn’t have noticed because it all seemed to go off so effortlessly.

As for the man himself? I spoke to him, but again, he didn’t have much to say, at least on the record. He seemed excited that I picked up on the intentional disharmony of the model routes, and explained that the space we were standing in was a “language I’ve been working on for 10 years” called “DROAM,” which refers to the minimalist design he hopes to apply to stores, urban planning, and a home for himself.

“I got a quote for you,” Victor interjected. “The king returns!” Ye laughed. The question remains, though: Is he welcome?

#6758. Kylie Jenner Has Called It: It’s Fawn Girl Fall

Kylie Jenner is no deer in the headlights, but she decided to go full fawn at the LACMA Art+Film Gala on Saturday night. Making her debut at the annual Los Angeles event to fundraise for the museum, the beauty mogul joined a starry crowd embracing all things glitzy and gloriously extravagant. For many, that meant a lot of sequins and skin-baring. But for Jenner, that meant a shimmering, body-skimming gown in fashion’s latest animal-print obsession: deer spots.

The dress, from Ashi Studio’s fall 2026 couture collection, was an on-trend departure from the usual leopard and zebra. Cut close to the body in a mottled chocolate-brown and silver fabric that resembled the delicate markings of a fawn, it featured a high halter neckline, a sculpted waist, and a floor-grazing skirt that flared gently from the knees. The original runway design featured tiny, sculptural antlers protruding from the collar, though these appear to have been removed for Jenner’s red-carpet outing.

It was also all business in the front, tassel in the back: the otherwise streamlined gown opened to reveal almost her entire back, with a swirling and shimmering tassel tracing down her spine. It was a little nod to the opulent, old-world glamour currently making its way back into fashion, which has been dominated by luxe detailing: swishing fringe, ornamental frog clasps, oversized bows, and fur-trimmed robes abound right now. More is more, particularly when it comes to the finer details.

Styled by Rose Grandquist and Mackenzie Grandquist, Jenner kept the rest of the look signature sultry. Hairstylist Igor Rosales-Jackson fashioned her jet-black lengths into a glossy, center-parted cascade of voluptuous waves, while makeup artist Ariel Tejada opted for fluttery lashes, softly bronzed cheeks, and a nude-pink lip. Zola Ganzorigt was behind her understated manicure, with jewelry by Lorraine Schwartz adding a final glint.

Jenner is hardly the first to go wild for the print. After years of leopard and zebra reigning supreme, fashion’s animal kingdom has welcomed a gentler, more woodland-inspired contender. Katie Holmes was an early adopter, stepping out in deer-spotted Tory Burch, while Sofia Richie Grainge gave the pattern her quiet-luxury seal of approval with a jacket and sleeveless maxi dress in the debut collection of her label, SRG. On the runways, the interpretations have been considerably more daring. For spring 2027, LaQuan Smith made Bambi print decidedly grown-up, working it into barely-there minidresses, sculpted jackets, and slinky combinations with flashes of lilac lingerie. Baum und Pferdgarten got in on the action by incorporating the motif into its playful, ballet-inspired collection. Elsewhere, British label Cawley Studio has taken a more heritage-minded approach, offering deer-spotted leather flying jackets and pillbox hats, while Carelli has brought the pattern into the realm of plush, statement-making outerwear.

There’s a surprising amount of versatility to the Bambi print. Where leopard has long carried a certain strain of bombshell bravado (remember the “mob wife” trend of yore?), deer spots feel softer and more romantic. Rendered in caramel and cream shades, it works particularly well with fall’s appetite for textures, suede, shearling, and rich, earthy tones. But, as Kylie Jenner proved, the print can look just as at home under the flashbulbs as it does on a countryside ramble

That was certainly the spirit of the evening. The 2026 LACMA Art+Film Gala red carpet was a veritable parade of shine, sparkle, and high-octane glamour, from Kim Kardashian’s oxblood Gucci sequins to the dramatic cutouts of Rosie Huntington-Whiteley. Jenner’s metallic deer look fit right in. This fall, fashion has a new creature to fawn over.

#6757. The Return of ‘Man At His Best’

A new (old) franchise to help guys steadily improve their lives emotionally, intellectually, and physically.

When my daughters, who are eight and eleven, tell me stories about the annoying behavior of the boys in their class, I like to roll my eyes and say, “Boys are the worst.”

That may be my own personal crisis. But did you know the American man is in crisis too? Of course you did.

For at least a decade, the media hasn’t let up: Men are lonely, friendless, and angry; falling behind in the workplace; dying deaths of despair. Outlets like The New York Times, The Atlantic, and, yes, Esquire have been dutifully diagnosing the problem for years.

Starting now, it’s time to offer solutions.

To do that, we’re restoring an Esquire franchise that began in the early 1980s—another time of crisis for American men. The male-dominated manufacturing industry was collapsing, women were entering the workplace and public life in larger numbers, divorce was on the rise, and men were expected to be more enlightened beings. It was all very confusing for guys, and it inspired melodramatic reactions.

Reactions like this, from Sam Keen’s New York Times best seller Fire in the Belly, which compared manhood to a night battle in the jungle: “Voices from the surrounding darkness shout hostile challenges: ‘Men are too aggressive. Too soft. . . . Too much like little boys.’ . . . Exactly what we are supposed to become is not clear.”

At the dawn of that decade, Esquire introduced a new slogan: Man at His Best. Two years later, it became a section in the magazine that would be a “reader’s resource for finding quality in everyday life.” That section was last seen in 2017, but to deliver those solutions, we’re reintroducing the franchise on Esquire.com, across our social channels, and in every print issue of Esquire. You’ll find a range of dispatches from multiple points of view—some of them from women—on both what it means to be a man in the 2020s and how to steadily improve your life emotionally, intellectually, and physically. We will publish at least one story a day on the topic; it will appear on the right side of our homepage, in our daily newsletter, and on the Man At His Best page.

Of course, the newly renovated Man at His Best is more than just eight pages in a print magazine. Here on Esquire.com, and you’ll see Man at His Best on the right side of the home page, with a new story every day. And you’ll see Man at His Best topics sprinkled across our social-media channels.

I try to be at my best when I’m with my daughters, and if the striving has taught me anything, it’s that this crisis will not resolve overnight. Growth takes time, at least eight or eleven years. But I’m certain Esquire can help. Don’t roll your eyes.

#6755. 21 Coats and Jackets I Think Are Cool Just Because

No contest, fall is the best season. For a few glorious months, it’s an open bar for dressing and getting your biggest fits off. Tell me what other season lets you go from flannel with cords to a hoodie with shorts to a puffer and jeans all in the same week. You can mix a wild cocktail of textures and colors, play recklessly with silhouettes and experiment to your heart’s content—and your wallet’s demise. But no doubt the best part of dressing for the best season is the outerwear.

And right now, the shelves are stocked with sick pieces, which means my tabs are so more packed than a Tokyo train during rush hour. From dramatic overcoats to slick truckers, artisanal macs and swishy windbreakers, the menswear gods are really smiling upon us right now. But why gab about how great this season’s roster of jackets and coats are when I can just show you? Here are the 21 coolest pieces of outerwear out right now.

Little Red Riding Hood was a menswear icon.

I didn't know you could wax corduroy. Now I do. And now I want it.

After decades of wearing clothes, I'm pretty convinced that reversible jackets are bad. Leave it to Niceness to be the very sick outlier.

This isn't totally my style but I'll figure out a way to make it work because it's just too cool to pass up.

Our Legacy just seems to be getting better and better.

I'm obsessed with Nosapluna, the mysterious and methodical design collective producing antique-inspired designs using artisanal and age-old techniques. Like, who needs Gore-tex when you have this?

Imagine this with a hoodie underneath and crazy faded baggy jeans. Pretty good.

Hoodies aren't normally categorized as outerwear. But then again, hoodies aren't normally as heavy as this, nor are they hand-knit by indigenous craftspeople. So, yeah.

Experiences are great. But if I have to choose between paying to fly to Montana or paying to LARP Montana, I'm going with this RRL jacket every time.

I did a review of Gap's heavy denim Type II jacket a while back and got accused of sponsored content. I meant that shit. And I mean this too: this is a pretty decent jacket that looks good and is reasonably priced.

It appears that the Dries team is doing just fine without Dries.

Boston-based indie label Mark the Tailor has the streets talking thanks to its balance of craftsmanship and a modern lens on tailoring. This playful flip on the humble quarter zip is just one of the things that has menswear fans buzzing.

Enough pockets for a 6-pack of Labatt Blue.

I'll be the first to say the pullover jackets are, on the whole, stupid. But there are always notable exceptions, like this sweet one from A Kind of Guise.

You could pay for top dollar for an authentic, vintage thrashed French chore coat. Or you could pay top dollar for a new, equally nice, hand-stitched French chore coat made specifically for the Self Edge 20th anniversary. The choice is yours.

Vintage heads will recognize this Buck piece as a retro revival of '30s jackets with its cropped silhouette, chain-zip chest pocket, and waist adjusters. The only thing it's missing is that vintage '30s aroma.

If the Chunnel were a garment, it would be this collaborative coat between A.P.C. and Barbour.

#6754. The Best Dressed Stars of the Week Weren’t Afraid to Play

A red carpet should, above all things, be fun. What is a step and repeat for anything other than to entertain and serve up a fashion fantasy? This week, the best dressed stars understood this assignment. Fun silhouettes brought an exciting energy back to the star-gazing space. No minimalism or stealthy-chic looks here: It was all about the bolder, the better.

Take last night’s LACMA Art + Film Gala. Supermodel Alex Consani hit the function in a black one-shouldered Gucci gown that featured an oversized, asymmetric neckline. Anya Taylor-Joy also went for volume in her vintage Pierre Cardin, which included a mega-ruffled duster coat.

In Miami, Hunter Schafer embraced bright neons in her upcycled NIHL hoodie and skirt—the perfect antithesis to earthy-tone fall dressing. Another fan of the artful clash? Sarah Paulson, who continued her All’s Fair press tour in a striped rugby shirt and embellished skirt from Michael Kors Collection—the perfect mix of high-low dressing. None of these looks were safe or expected, and thank god for that! We’d rather risk-taking than a total snoozefest.

#6751. Our 11 Favorite Watches Coming to the Biggest Auctions of the Year

Want more insider watch coverage? Get Box + Papers, GQ's newsletter devoted to the watch world, sent to your inbox every Friday. Sign up here to get it free.

This is the biggest weekend of the year for vintage watches. It’s the year-end watch auctions in Geneva, where many prestigious houses bring their very best pieces to market. And it’s never been a more enthralling time to keep a close eye on what happens in Geneva over the next few days. In the first half of the year, the number of million-dollar watches nearly eclipsed the total for the entirety of 2025. A couple of the pieces listed below, including a unique Rolex and a rare Patek Philippe in stainless steel, have estimates above a million bucks.

Writer Oren Hartov and I pored over hundreds of lots to bring you our 11 favorite watches plus one bonus selection. See them all below.

You know a banger is coming up for sale when the house behind it doesn’t even bother capping its price range. Auction estimates are routinely and famously low to encourage bidders, and this watch’s starting point is still $1.2 million. Why? Well, have you ever seen a Rolex like this before? Before Rolex defined the look of modern watches with pieces like the Submariner, it operated similarly to many other manufacturers in Switzerland, willing to make one-off pieces and experiment frequently with its design.

This square beauty from the early 1940s is “most probably unique,” as Phillips auction house writes in its essay on the piece. This exact piece last hit the auction block in 2004, and no other example has come up for public sale since. It’s crazy to see how much this watch’s case shape resembles Heuer’s similarly blocky Monaco, which wouldn’t be released for another 25-plus years. Unfortunately, as cool as this watch is, it does not come with onyx prayer beads. —Cam Wolf

There’s Patek, then there’s complicated Patek, then there’s stainless steel complicated Patek, then there’s stainless steel complicated Patek made in just a handful of examples, then there’s stainless steel complicated Patek made in just a handful of examples in insane condition. This watch checks all those boxes. A reference 1436, it’s a split-seconds (rattrapante) chronograph, meaning it can time successive intervals of a race or event. One of just two stainless steel examples known to the market, it has an estimate of $2.4-$4.8M, a testament to its rarity and importance. —Oren Hartov

Yet another rare watch executed in stainless steel, this fabulous Lange 1 boasts a gorgeous two-tone dial in blue, with darker subdials contrasting against a cobalt-colored main dial. Dating to 1999 and first sold by the German retailer Oeding-Erdel, it’s one of approximately 30 pieces made in the most utilitarian of metals. Originally fitted with a more standard silvered dial, it received its current navy-blue dial as a replacement and is one of just two stainless steel Lange 1s known in this particular configuration. —OH

Renewed interest in Urban Jürgensen stemming from its recent relaunch under the directorship of Kari Voutilainen, who has since left the CEO position but remains on the company’s board, has seen watches such as this early-’90s ref. 2 garner more attention. A lovely perpetual calendar-moonphase, it’s housed in a classically inspired 37.7mm yellow gold case with cornes-de-vache-style lugs, a stepped bezel, and an incredible dial with the brand’s signature observatory-style hands. Someone tell Timothée Chalamet. —OH

Chopard has a hard-earned reputation for putting out some of the most finely made watches in Switzerland. It’s not just the nerds who are familiar with its work anymore, either. If we (the nerds, obviously) were sending a watch in a bottle to help share that message far and wide, this Lunar One, which looks like something out of Superman’s icy Fortress of Solitude, wouldn’t be a bad choice. This is Chopard’s first watch to combine a perpetual calendar and a moonphase, which is like shaving truffles on caviar. I love that the Roman numerals at 4 and 8 o’clock look like columns nearly buckling under the weight of the center of the dial. This watch also comes with several fun add-ons, like onyx prayer beads plus a ring and a pen set with diamonds. —Cam Wolf

While many younger collectors are obsessed with the Cosmograph Daytona, true “Crown” heads know that other pre-Daytona chronographs sometimes present an even more compelling proposition. This ref. 3525 ‘’Bariletto,’ dating to the 1940s, is not only the first Oyster-cased Rolex chronograph, but it’s also the only known stainless-steel example carrying the signature on the dial of Proud’s, a Rolex retailer based in Sydney. Manually wound, paired to a handsome beads-of-rice bracelet, and measuring a compact 36mm, it comes from the collection of important Italian collector Pucci Papaleo. —OH

While this stainless steel Patek may look like a normal ref. 2509—a beautiful hand-wound dress watch from the midcentury—it’s actually a “school watch” modified by a watchmaking student at the Geneva Watchmaking School. Dating to the 1960s, it’s housed in a 35mm stainless steel case and features a lovely dial with the ‘Ecole d’Horlogerie Geneve’ signature instead of Patek Philippe’s. Open it up, and the hand-wound movement is signed by Norbert Henry, the watchmaking student who assembled and finished it. While it may not attract the attention of more typical Patek collectors, its under-the-radar qualities make it a potential sleeper hit. —OH

It’s tough to argue with the sheer beauty of Vacheron’s mid-20th-century output, much of which is vastly underappreciated compared to comparable pieces from the likes of Patek Philippe. This splendid yellow gold ref. 4072 with a two-tone multi-scale dial dates to the late 1940s—one of my favorite eras of watch design. Powered by the hand-wound cal. V 492 movement and featuring a lovely set of long, contoured lugs, its dial is in fantastic condition, with applied dart and Roman indices, sharp printing, a crisp signature, and legible tachymeter and telemeter scales. It will surely find its way onto the wrist of a collector with excellent taste. —OH

This watch’s dial depicts Saint George, who, according to legend, slew a dragon while on horseback. This is a perfect use for the rich, deep colors you get from enamel. The flames licking at Saint George are beautiful shades of orange and red. He triumphantly lifts his spear as his steed rears its front legs. It’s very cool how much story you can get from this little 35mm timepiece. —CW

Watch collectors might pony up a few thousand for one of independent watchmaker F.P. Journe’s used tissues at this point. However, they’ll have to settle for a host of accessories coming to auction instead this weekend. The maker is so in-demand that, in addition to his timepieces, houses are selling his empty watch boxes and a set of toys that resemble him. This lot is in the middle of those two extremes: a wall clock made to resemble Journe’s Octa Réserve de Marche. Although I’m not gonna lie, flipping this over and seeing the compartment where you stuff in the batteries is a bit of a buzzkill. —CW

They used to make everything look more elegant. This original Longines design was developed in 1931 with famous aviator Charles Lindbergh. It is technically a pilot’s watch, but its elegant, icy-blue dial and Roman numerals would make it the fanciest model on many red carpets in 2026. This is a model from the ‘80s inspired by that original design, and it comes on an absolutely righteous beads-of-rice bracelet. Someone is going to get this guy for around $2,500 if the estimate is correct! —CW

In Rolex world, even the advertisements sell for thousands of dollars. It’s hard to blame people when we’re talking about a rare poster of a GMT-Master wearing a snow-dusted Rolex beanie. Awwww. (Relatedly, imagine if Rolex sold that beanie!? Oh, boy.) —CW

#6750. No Time to Dye: Jacob Elordi Goes Blonde

The name’s Blonde. James Blonde. Kidding: it’s Jacob Elordi, who has just added another hairstyle to his ever-expanding beauty repertoire. The actor, whose dark, tousled hair has become almost as recognizable as his collection of Bottega Veneta bags, appears to have taken a trip to the bleach bottle.

In photos obtained by Deuxmoi, Elordi was spotted attending a performance of Paranormal Activity on Broadway in New York City on Saturday evening, alongside girlfriend Kendall Jenner. While the Australian actor (who is reportedly in the running to be the next James Bond) kept a low profile in a black beanie, there was no disguising the sandy blonde strands peeking out from beneath it. It’s a significant change-up from his usual chocolate-brown waves, though the hat leaves the full extent of his transformation something of a mystery.

Of course, Elordi is no stranger to experimenting in the grooming department. There was the shaggy, bushy beard he debuted at the Marrakech International Film Festival in 2024, followed by the rather rakish mutton chops from turn as Heathcliff in Wuthering Heights. More recently, he’s returned to the mustache and the artfully disheveled, ’90s-inflected mullet, while also dabbling in a goatee. Jacob Elordi, it seems, has never met a divisive men’s grooming trend he couldn’t make look good.

There’s probably a cinematic explanation for his latest transformation. Elordi is currently shooting Scapegoat, the forthcoming A24 film from Midsommar and Hereditary director Ari Aster, alongside Scarlett Johansson and Jude Law. The film reportedly follows a surgeon whose career comes under fire after a social media influencer dies during a routine operation. Details of the project remain tightly under wraps, and whether his new color is character-related is anyone’s guess. Still, considering his commitment to transforming his appearance for previous roles, it’s likely.

Kendall Jenner is well placed to offer a little blonde advice. In September 2024, the model traded her own signature brunette for a golden, Carolyn Bessette-Kennedy-inspired blonde, courtesy of colorist Jenna Perry. She has also experimented with fiery copper hair.

Whether this is a fleeting flirtation with peroxide or the beginning of a new beauty era, one thing is certain: Jacob Elordi is keeping us on our toes. And we’ve only had a glimpse of the blonde ambition beneath that beanie.

#6748. My Life as an Asylum Seeker in the U.S.

I came here 11 years ago to give my daughter a better life. I believe in the American dream, even if the American government doesn’t want me here.

I want to tell you about some things that I think you can only understand when you are an immigrant.

The first, and most important, is that emigrating is not something you do without a reason to leave. I will tell you mine. In Venezuela, when I would take my daughter to school, she had to ride lying down on the floor of the car. At any moment, someone might knock on your door, point a gun, steal your phone. It was safer to have her flat on the ground, below the windows. She was a great student at a private school, and that is what it took to get her there. I challenge you to imagine being a father and seeing that little girl, not even ten years old, huddling for safety.

That was my reason for leaving, but it is not the reason I and my family have been allowed to stay here. We are asylum seekers, and there are strict rules around qualifying for asylum in the United States. The fear of being mugged is not enough. But political persecution is. In the year after the 2013 election of President Nicolás Maduro, when life in Venezuela was very difficult, the country erupted in protests. I was among the protesters, and I was detained and separated from my family for a week. We decided that when we visited my sister in Miami in 2015, we would request asylum.

This is surely something you only understand as an immigrant: the specific, and confusing, rules and requirements and procedures of the American immigration system. People who are born here can take these things for granted. They don’t understand how much of your life can be dictated by paperwork and how the paperwork your life most depends on always has the most boring name. When we got to the United States, the application for asylum I filled out and turned in to U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services, a part of the Department of Homeland Security, was called Form I-589.

According to the government, it should have taken at most five months for the application to be processed and to get an interview, which would allow USCIS to evaluate if my family should be granted asylum.

Our wait began when I turned in that form. That was the start of the first countdown clock. You think about it every day, because for those five months, you cannot work. When they are up, you can fill out another form, Form I-765, to apply for a work permit. But in the meantime: Five months… four months… three months…

We were fortunate: We had savings. Miami was expensive, but we were getting by.

As the clock ticked down, we had a decision to make. We had family in Miami, but it was too expensive for us to stay for the long term. If the process dragged on much longer, we’d run out of money. We decided to move north, to Orlando. We didn’t know anyone there, but it was affordable. That’s where we would wait out our chance at the American dream.

When we moved there, the newest iPhone was the iPhone 6s. A nuclear deal was finalized with Iran. Barack Obama was president.

Eleven years later, we are still waiting for an interview.

Right now, when many people here think about immigration, they think about ICE—men in the streets with guns, killing people in Minnesota, or Maine, or Texas. I worry about ICE every day, but what has defined the past decade of my life is the waiting. Maybe if I can tell you about it, you will understand something, even a small part, of what it is to be an immigrant.

In Orlando, we were alone. We moved in December, a difficult month. Christmas is a big holiday in Venezuela, and there the family is always together: cousins, siblings, uncles, aunts, grandparents. Our first Christmas was just the three of us.

I dutifully filled out Form I-765. I understood the work permit would take about two weeks to arrive. Once I had it, another countdown: It would be good only for one year. In that time, though, I could get a job and also a driver’s license, which would make our lives much easier. And surely, we thought, a year was enough time for our interview appointment to come through.

Instead of two weeks, the permit took three months. Three more months of stretching our savings. There were desperate moments. We sometimes had to go to churches to get food so we wouldn’t starve. We wondered if we should go home, live with the risks in Venezuela. Finding resolve in these moments is hard. Having a young child motivates you, but you also see the challenges they face. My daughter was nine years old when we arrived. She had anxiety attacks when she first started school, which was in a different language and organized much differently from her school in Venezuela.

When my work permit finally arrived, we were so happy. This card with the faded flag and my picture and the red border—we felt that we could sustain ourselves.

It wasn’t so easy. My English is not perfect. It isn’t now, and it really wasn’t when I started looking for jobs. I’m an engineer by training. I worked at a telephone company in Venezuela. When I first started working here in the United States, I worked overnight, I cleaned bathrooms, I cleaned kitchens, I washed cars. I’m not trying to denigrate those jobs; they were the first jobs that I could find. But I could not get paid well doing them. After we had been here for a year, our savings ran out. We were lucky to have family and friends who could help us. But we kept going to food pantries. I always tried to make sure that my daughter and my wife did not go without food. I often didn’t eat enough myself.

After we had been here for a few years, my mom came to the United States to visit me and my sister. It was the first time she had seen me in four years. I was so skinny she cried.

I did some English classes online, but they did not really work. Here is another thing you understand when you are an immigrant: When you have to start to speak on the street, it’s very different from the lessons that they teach you in class. Really, construction job sites were my classroom. With more English, I became more confident I could find a job in my field.

Before I could do that, my work permit expired. I applied for a renewal, and I got another one. Another year. Another countdown until the day I could, hopefully, make my family’s case.

By then, President Obama had left office, but before he did his administration made work permits valid for two years. That was what my next renewal got me—a little more time to work, and save, and wait. But it also made me think the government might expect us to be waiting two more years.

Meanwhile, Donald Trump had been elected president. I wasn’t blind to his attacks on immigrants, but my family and I were following the rules, working hard, just trying to survive. And Venezuelans, historically, hadn’t immigrated that much to the United States. We didn’t think the attacks were about us.

But things were changing. More and more people were coming from Venezuela and from other countries in South and Central America. My family thought of ourselves as three people looking for safety, but we could tell we were becoming something different: a problem.

We started to see news that the people who were waiting for asylum interviews were waiting four years. Later, it became five years. And then, as you started to talk to people, they tell you that they’ve been waiting six years or they’ve been waiting seven years.

It was hard to imagine how we could possibly last that long, but in 2019 I saw a listing for a job in my old profession. It was with a major telecommunications company. I was hired to join a team that climbs up telecom towers to do maintenance and upgrades. Back in Venezuela, I had supervised this kind of work.

My daughter was in high school by this time, and I would think about her when I was up there. When she was little, she would tell me she wanted to be an engineer. I told her, You don’t have to be an engineer just because I’m an engineer. It could be scary being up so high. We have harnesses, and something like parachutes, and we’re always connected to something in case we fall, but we recognize that we can’t get too comfortable, because any error could end our lives. Still, there was something special about being able to see for miles, this place that held my family’s future stretching out in every direction.

Most of us on the crew were new, many of us immigrants. Our boss was impressed at the quality of our work. He asked us once, How is it that you guys are able to do this kind of work not having done it before? I told him we were trained. And also that when you have this need to survive, you have this need to get ahead, you end up finding a way.

For years we had been saving, and Covid made it possible for us to save much more. The pandemic, strangely, was good for my family. I was an essential worker, and I received bonuses and other incentives. I never stopped working. At the same time, Covid exposed the political problems I protested in Venezuela, which made the pandemic even worse there. It was a reminder of why we had left.

And the house was a reminder of home. In Venezuela, people move less than they do here. Neighbors stay for years, for a very long time. The importance of a house there, like here, is that when you own it, no one can remove you from it. It really meant something to feel that feeling in America—like we were beginning to live the American dream. My daughter, in her way, had even become a typical American teenager. Our new house was about forty minutes from where we had been living, so she had to change schools. She sulked.

In 2023, the Biden administration extended work permits from two years to five years. I think probably they did this because, after the pandemic, everything was chaos. I knew it was a sign that my family might be waiting unimaginably longer for our interview, but when I renewed my permit in 2024, after living life in a five-month increment, then one-year increments, then two-year increments, five years felt like forever, like a clock it was hard to imagine reaching zero.

I won’t tell you that it all came crashing down when President Trump was elected a second time. It’s not just that Orlando wasn’t like Minnesota. There was no crash. It was a gradual decline in freedom and a gradual increase in fear.

Simply, here is what began to happen this past December and January, when things got bad: You’re driving on the highway and you’re followed by an undercover cop. Sometimes it’s for a few minutes, sometimes it’s for ten minutes or more. Sometimes they pull you over. Sometimes they detain you.

In Florida, many law-enforcement agencies collaborate with ICE, so almost anywhere you go is a risk. I drive a lot for work, and I see enforcement in exits and rest stops and Wawas, in school areas where you have to go slow. There are police or highway patrol or border patrol on the turnpike down to Miami, and on State Road 417, and on Interstate 4. You can be referred to ICE if you owe money for a toll, or if you don’t stop for a stop sign, or if they see that your driver’s license says that it’s temporary. Unlike most people, I like working more than fifty miles from home—it means I can stay in a hotel, which means less driving.

Going to work, or for essentials, is nearly all we do. When my family needs groceries, only my wife goes or only I go. We can’t risk both being picked up, because of my daughter. As for my daughter, she sometimes has my sister—a lawful permanent resident who moved to Orlando after we did—drive her to school.

There are a lot of people in my situation in this part of Florida, so we find ways to help each other. We have chat groups, maybe fifteen hundred people total, that warn each other about high-risk areas. And I am a member of an organization called the Asylum Seeker Advocacy Project that has helped us understand our rights and how to be safe.

Thank God, I have never been stopped. But my wife and I each keep a binder in the car just in case. We know it might not be worth a lot, but we carry it with us. It contains all of our paperwork, the forms with boring names that are proof we have a right to be here. Our immigration paperwork, our asylum applications, the approvals for work permits that we’ve gotten before, the asylum receipts and claims. Everything we might need in case one of us is detained. You have to basically see if the documentation convinces the police officer to let you go. But it is up to luck. It is up to God.

Sometimes a risk is worth it to feel that you are still living.

Once, I took a trip to a bar with a few friends. Three beers and an Uber home. It was so scary, but we did it.

The gym, four days a week, at 4:30 a.m.—before law enforcement is on the road. Once or twice a week, when her schedule allows, my daughter comes. She has the certifications to be a personal trainer, so she’s my personal trainer. There comes an age, though, at which children don’t really want to spend that much time with their parents, so she just tells me what to do and goes to do her own exercise. I still like having her there. I’ve lost about forty-three pounds, roughly twenty kilos, over the last year and a half. This time by choice.

Then there was the World Baseball Classic, in Miami last March. I love baseball. When Venezuela reached the semis, I knew I had to go. We left at 3:00 a.m. for the four-hour drive down. Venezuela beat Italy in the semis, so we stayed for the final. Of all the teams we could have faced, it turned out to be the U.S.A. The game was in the evening, and it ended late in the night. We drove directly back to Orlando.

Venezuela ended up champions, by the way. It was like vengeance, because the United States knocked us out in the quarterfinals of the last WBC, in 2023. And to top it off, my favorite player, Wilyer Abreu, hit a home run in the championship game. He’s from Maracaibo, just like me.

We have an ongoing joke with the people we know who are also in limbo. We’ll casually refer to “when we were treated like U.S. citizens.” Now we’re treated like criminals, but in other times, in other administrations, we could make a life without worrying so much, the way that we do now. Still, my family does our best to live like U.S. citizens. We follow the rules. I would not have a job, for example, if Immigration had not given me a work permit with which to do that job. I know, because for eight months, I did not work—I went hungry. We pay taxes on our house. I pay taxes on what I make at my job. I’ve always paid. I’ve been here eleven years now, making a life, paying taxes to the government, but I still am here with no status. Who is the criminal?

I guess it’s not really a joke. I can tell you that if you were an immigrant, you would understand.

Since things got really bad in December and January, they haven’t gotten much worse, but they also haven’t gotten better. We stick to our routine: work, groceries, school.

Recently, one of the places that I was going to have to service for my job was a police station, and I told my boss that I could not do it. I told him that he should change me out for a different job, and that if he didn’t I would stay at home until I could be assigned to a different site. He was able to find something safer for me to do. He is a very understanding man. Several of us are in the same situation, and the company has been very supportive.

So many people down here are like that. In my experience, the politicians do not make a country. The people do.

And so through everything, my feelings toward this country have not changed. I will stand on the fact that this is a great country. I’m very thankful. The situation in Venezuela was not good. Some people tell me that things are better there now, since the U.S. detained President Maduro. I’m not hopeful. I am grateful for the peace we’ve had here. I came for a better life for my family and for my daughter. We bought our house; we have saved for our daughter’s future.

Eleven years is far too long to live someplace and still be made to feel like an outsider, let alone like a criminal. That is the thinking of someone who takes home for granted. But I am an immigrant. One thing I understand is how to extend grace to a place that is foreign to me. I have nothing against the U.S. I am grateful for this country.

At the end of last year, for the first time since I have lived here, the government made work permits shorter. Now they last only eighteen months. The wait has not gotten any shorter, though. We’ve seen no signs we’ll get an interview anytime soon. I was very lucky to get a five-year permit when I did. Right now, my countdown runs until 2029.

If there is one thing I am certain Americans who were born here do not understand, it is the immigration system itself. I have been telling you about the past decade of my life and our excruciating wait for our asylum interview. I have not told you yet that that is not the end of the process.

After our interview, we will wait for a decision. Officially, it should take only two weeks. I know it will take longer. It will be a long time still that we live with the question that, for eleven years now, has been hanging over our heads: What if we do not get to stay? But in a way, after all this time building a life here, the uncertainty of that question has lost some of its power. If I’m honest with you, when my daughter is ready to graduate college, I can tell you that I could die in peace, because she’s my only daughter, and what I wanted most for her was a good future.

A long time ago, she changed her mind about being an engineer. After she started taking college classes, she decided to study something called media design. She’s learning how to create applications, like for phones. She graduates in May.

I still cannot believe that when we got here, she was just nine years old. It’s painful for me, as it is for any father, to look nostalgically back at when this grown woman was my little girl. But it also fills me with joy. My wife and I have spent every minute of every hour of every day of all of the time since she was young counting down—to the exhaustion of our savings, to the end of a work permit, to an interview. You persevere through these things for your children for a simple reason. Children should only ever have to count up.

#6747. GQ’s 13 Breakout Stars of 2026

Sometimes it’s fun to be early to the party. GQ launched the Breakouts portfolio in 2014 to celebrate the Hollywood upstarts who were poised to do big things. And not to brag, but we nailed it; that first group included Miles Teller, Shailene Woodley, Eddie Redmayne, and the late, great Chadwick Boseman. Over the ensuing years, we featured plenty more soon-to-be-superstars: Rami Malek. Brie Larson. Daniel Kaluuya. Riz Ahmed. Barry Keoghan. The kids from Stranger Things, when they were still kids. The cast of Succession before Succession became everyone’s favorite show.

In 2017, we put a baby-faced Timothée Chalamet on the list for his turn in Call Me by Your Name. (Our global entertainment director, Dana Mathews, fondly recalls him turning to her during the Man of the Year Party and saying, “This is the best party I’ve ever been to in my life.”) Since then, Chalamet has appeared on three GQ covers, earned four Oscar nominations, and become a household name (and maybe been to a few more great parties).

We took a few years off (okay, fine, seven), but 2026 feels like exactly the right time to revive GQ’s Breakouts portfolio—now through a wider lens. Yes, though we’ve got eyes on Hollywood’s next big things—like, say, Sly Stallone doppelgänger Anthony Ippolito; Gen Z class clown Owen Thiele, of Adults; Misty Green’s astounding leading woman, Rosalind Eleazar—not everyone is working the camera. We’re excited to introduce you to the West Coast’s hottest up-and-coming rapper in AZ Chike and put you on to Fcukers, whose debut album, packed with rowdy electro-pop bangers, made them first in our hearts and on our pregaming playlists. We’ve also got podcaster and journalist Pablo Torre, whose relentless reporting upended a $7.8 billion NBA franchise, and Jordan Firstman, an internet-born comedian who wrote and directed a film that commanded a lengthy standing ovation from Cannes audiences (right after they finished crying).

Point is, our Breakouts class of 2026 brings together 13 fully minted stars who did something that feels increasingly impossible: They captured our attention in a time when it feels like attention is more fleeting than ever. Welcome to their party.

Dress by Dior. Shoes by Jimmy Choo. Mask from Palace Costume Co.

Age: 25Breakout moment: Playing the queen bee on Ryan Murphy’s ’80s glam fever dream The Shards.—————

It’s a different kind of attention that I actually prefer. Because for so long I was getting attention, but not for a specific thing. And that was confusing and kind of messed with my head a bit. I was really young and people knew who I was, but I couldn’t really point to the work that they knew. And so it’s really fun for me to have people [now say], “I watched The Shards,” or “I watched Bottoms,” and then we have something to talk about.

Infinite Jest—no, I’m kidding, they’ve already read it, all of them. A Man’s Place by Annie Ernaux is very good and easily digestible. I think Just Kids is wonderful. What We Talk About When We Talk About Love. That one’s really great. Oh, and this is so classic, but Nine Stories by J.D. Salinger is really good. I know guys—male actors especially—love The Catcher in the Rye.

I got really worried the other day because I started getting a lot of followers. It was two days of so many followers, and I was like, “Oh my God, I’ve been doxxed.” The last thing I logged was Hitch. My top four are A Woman Under the Influence, The Dark Knight, Phantom Thread, and Eternal Sunshine. My Odyssey review has 112 likes. I don’t care how many followers I have on Instagram, how many likes I get. Letterboxd is truly a hit of adrenaline every time someone likes my review. —Frazier Tharpe

Jacket and jeans by Ralph Lauren Collection. Necklace by Chopard. Ring by Chanel Fine Jewelry.

On Wise: Jacket by Isabel Marant. Top by Gucci. Briefs by Araks. Boots by Herbert Levine. Sunglasses by McQueen. On Walker Lewis: Jacket by Balenciaga. T-shirt by Isabel Marant. Jeans by Gucci. Boots by Timberland. Sunglasses by Tom Ford. Jewelry, his own.

Ages: Wise, 28 | Walker Lewis, 29Breakout Moment: The NYC duo’s 2026 debut album, Ö, featuring indie-sleazy hits like “If You Wanna Party, Come Over to My House” and “Beatback.”—————

Wise: That was probably the most surreal thing I’ve ever experienced. We’re like, “This is what it feels to be like Led Zeppelin.”

Walker Lewis: It’s funny—a reel permeated my Instagram from a Brazilian influencer, and it was like, “Who is this controversial band that everyone’s arguing about opening for Harry Styles?” But I think by the last show, people got it.

Walker Lewis: Easy. The Cure. It’s unbelievable, to see somebody still sound that good and be able to play for two hours, and you know every single song.

Walker Lewis: When I was getting a root canal done and the nurse said, “Can I get a photo with you after?” I was like, “You couldn’t have asked before?” —Alex Pappademas

(from l.) On Firstman: All clothing by Tom Ford. Earrings, his own. On Walker Lewis: Jacket by Louis Vuitton Men’s. Shirt and sunglasses by Tom Ford. Tie by Our Legacy. Necklace, his own. On Wise: Top and pants by McQueen.

Robe by Dolce & Gabbana. Pants by Lu’u Dan. Watch by Cartier. Earring, his own.

Age: 28Breakout Moment: The series Off Campus, as the hottest fictional hockey player from this year’s hottest fictional hockey show.—————

I cannot shut up about this, but it has to be throwing the first pitch out for the White Sox. I will remember that forever.

Yeah, it was. And I hadn’t thrown a baseball in a really long time.

I look forward to the moment where I get to really reflect and digest. Next month I have some time off, and I’m going to go home and eat sandwiches at my mom’s house and take my grandma for a walk. “Go on a walk with my grandma”.… That’s a weird way to put it.

I’m, like, an idiot. I’m a full goofball. Garrett Graham is the heartthrob. To me, I’m just like, “I’m Bel.” And in my head, those are very different things. I’m flattered that people can associate me with heartthrob status, but no, I don’t wake up in the morning feeling like a heartthrob.

I mean, I always wanted to play Holden Caulfield, but who knows? —Trishna Rikhy

Jacket and pants by Prada. Shirt by Brioni. Pocket square by Charvet. Belt by Artemas Quibble. Sunglasses by Jacques Marie Mage. Necklace and ring by David Yurman.

Jacket by McQueen. Shirt by Factor’s. Pants by Versace. Boots by Tom Ford. Sunglasses (throughout) by Louis Vuitton Men’s. Earrings (throughout), his own.

Age: 30Breakout Moment: Being the infectiously charismatic friend-to-all on FX’s zoomer sitcom Adults.—————

Sadie Sink knew who I was, and that was kind of cool. I just love her. She’s so talented and so adorable. It’s like meeting the queen before she’s the queen.

I do watch the fan edits. They’re fun. Some of them pick the worst photos of me, and I’m like, “This is a hate crime, but thank you for putting it on TikTok.”

I got two very smart pieces of advice. One was, “Run. Don’t do this. Save yourself.” And then the other person said, “Stick with it.” I’m kind of doing both. I am simultaneously sticking with it and trying my hardest, but also I’m like, Once you have a win, you do have to celebrate it and run as far away as you can and hide.

I bought a bag from The Row…which looks like—and I say this with love—it could be $20, but it’s the most expensive thing I own. And I did this because I went shopping with Hailey Bieber, and when you’re shopping with Hailey Bieber you buy things you think you can afford but you probably can’t…and now it’s too late to return. It’s a beautiful bag—it’s quiet luxury, babe. It’s so quiet you don’t know it’s The Row. —F.T

Jacket and pants by Saint Laurent by Anthony Vaccarello. Boots by Giuseppe Zanotti. Sunglasses (throughout) by Louis Vuitton Men’s. Earrings (throughout), his own. Ring by Bvlgari.

Dress by Bottega Veneta. Shoes by Herbert Levine. Sunglasses by Celine.

Age: 38Breakout moment: Her riveting performance as the title character in Chris Rock’s Misty Green (and her role in Slow Horses).—————

I mean, the first time I watched it, I just thought, Oh—you’re going to be in every frame. [Laughs]

[In an American accent] “Murderer.” Mur-der-rer. I think every Brit finds that hard. I was like, “Can I say ’killer’ instead?” And “mirror.” It’s when you’ve got a double r. But I had a great dialect coach.

I would’ve loved to have been in a scene with Philip Seymour Hoffman. That would’ve been my dream. And I would love to work with Sandra Hüller.

I was onstage with Ralph Fiennes. We finished Misty Green—I did an overnight shoot on Friday into Saturday morning, got on a plane, arrived in London on Sunday, and went straight into rehearsals with Ralph. It was a pretty mad summer.

I was getting ready before the Misty Green premiere [at the Toronto International Film Festival]. And my mom came down. She sat there and she was just sending pictures and she just had tears in her eyes. Just seeing this whole period at TIFF—for her, it’s her little girl. And every now and again, I would just look at her and she was just happy and in awe in a way. It warmed my heart. —A.P.

Dress by Gucci. Hosiery by Wolford. Earrings by Cartier.

Shirt and pants by Brioni. Bow tie and cummerbund, stylist’s own. Vintage watch by Rolex from Foundwell. Vintage cufflinks by Cartier from Foundwell. Earring, his own.

Age: 35Breakout moment: The Cannes hit Club Kid, which he wrote, directed, and starred in as a party promoter navigating unexpected parenthood.—————

I still do, yeah, at the phone call scene at the end. But it feels very distant from me. I feel like I’m watching it more as an observer now, which is nice, and I feel different than when I made it. I was such an open wound.

Cannes was such an emotional experience. I’m 35, and I’ve always known that I had something to say and I knew how to say it, but I’ve never been given the opportunity. So, honestly, to feel like I was being seen and understood was like 20 years of validation that I didn’t get. And so something shifted, that week, in me. I’ve noticed myself not having to use humor as a shield anymore, as much. I’m less afraid to be vulnerable—and not just in my public life but in my personal life too.

Of course, you shouldn’t need the validation of anyone to feel like you’re worthy, but let’s be real.…

What gagged me this year? I would say, honestly, as a statement of ambition, the Javis’ movie [La Bola Negra]. You marvel at it because you’re like, “How the fuck did they pull this off?” To even want to tell that complex of a story, and to just do it and go balls to the wall, is very inspiring.

I was like, “This is too long. It’s embarrassing now.” —A.P.

Jacket and pants by Canali. Shirt by Amiri. Boots by Alessandro Vasini. Tie by Husbands.

Age: 41Breakout moment: Reporting on how the Steve Ballmer–owned Clippers were allegedly funny with money, on his podcast Pablo Torre Finds Out, leading to one of the most severe team penalties in sports history.—————

Two days ago, I walked into this event that The New York Times was holding…it was like the 175th birthday party [for the paper]. I walk out the elevator and literally the first person I see is [NBA commissioner] Adam Silver. I won’t say exactly what he told me, but the tenor of our conversation was like, This is the HBO series adaptation of what this moment would be.

As a first-generation American—my parents are from the Philippines—there’s always been a dream of mine to be cast as a white person. So…Andrew Garfield, come on. Let’s do this.

The funny part is that I’m not even done reporting this story yet. The federal government is now investigating the Clippers, and so I’m now investigating the government’s investigation in the era of Trump too, which is like its own rabbit hole inside of a rabbit hole, which is fucking wild. But at the same time, it feels like now our number is listed in the phone book…actual other NBA owners are calling me up saying, “Can you look into this?”

It’s hard not to be sappy about this, but the lesson I learned is that if you’re telling the truth, you can walk into any room and feel like that as a suit of armor. Even when the person you’re investigating is one of the 10 richest people in the world. —F.T.

Coat by Michael Kors. Vintage pajamas from Palace Costume Co. Socks by London Sock Company. Glasses by Jacques Marie Mage. Necklaces (throughout), his own.

Age: 37Breakout moments: Stealing scenes as a ’70s Provincetown line cook in the Anthony Bourdain biopic Tony, and his stand-up special Uncle Stav.—————

I just did The Drew Barrymore Show. That experience was so magical. I was so nervous to be around Drew Barrymore. I’ve done a lot of cool shit, and that’s the one where I was like, “I am actually nervous to the point where I’m not a professional. I’m just a stammering little boy who’s with the girl he had a crush on from The Wedding Singer when he was a fat 10-year-old, and I’m trying to keep it together.”

Last week I allowed myself an aimlessly wander around New York City day. Got a little stoned, walked around, stumbled into a movie. Walked along the water on the West Side. Sat down to a little random omakase. Rode a Citi Bike around. I call it the hero’s journey, where you leave your home at, whatever, 11 a.m. ,with just the bare provisions, and you’re not allowed to go home. You just have to keep moving and keep doing stuff.

I filmed this Judd Apatow movie The Comeback King, with Glen Powell, Cristin Milioti, Madelyn Cline. That comes out in February. I’m excited to do stand-up—for fun, not to explicitly work on another hour. I’m excited to go back to clubs and just like, “Can I be the funniest person in this club tonight?” And that’s my only goal.

To be honest with you, the last three years, it’s [been] all go. But you got to have these big years, or else GQ doesn’t talk to you at the end of the year. —A.P.

On Halkias: Jacket and pants by Brooks Brothers. Shirt by Many. Shoes by Louis Vuitton Men’s. Sunglasses by Valention. On Torre: Jacket by Tom Ford. Shirt by Factor’s. Pants by Louis Vuitton Men’s. Shoes by G.H. Bass. Sunglasses by Jacques Marie Mage. Ring, his own.

Shirts and pants by Dunhill. Underwear by Calvin Klein. Earrings (throughout), his own.

Age: 31Breakout moment: Storming the West Coast rap scene with collabs from Pharrell Williams and Tyler, the Creator on his major-label debut album, No Rest for the Wicked.—————

Not like I made it, but I have arrived. We went to Magic City on a Monday for the first time. They were playing the fuck out my records in that motherfucker. The DJ played “Look Like My Mama” in the strip club. You ain’t never heard Tyler, the Creator get played in a strip club. We crossing worlds that’s never been crossed before.

The day before the album came out, we were in Area 29 in Houston, doing our thing. Regular night, it ain’t too packed, throwing money. They tap me on my shoulder like, “My boy want to holler at you.” They take me upstairs to this private section, pull the curtain back…it’s Travis Scott.

It was epic, bro. N-gga came out from behind the curtain like Batman. The light hid half his face. He said, “I fuck with everything you got going on.” We go back down to that section, 15 minutes pass, then one of the owners came and grabbed me: “Look, look, look.” Travis was up there, playing [Chike’s song] “Packed Up.” —F.T.

Shirt by Lu’u Dan. Pants by Valentino. Bracelet by Cartier.

Age: 27Breakout moment: Being a dead ringer for Sly Stallone in I Play Rocky, the film about…Sly Stallone playing Rocky.—————

In the thick of prep. I was training at Gleason’s Gym with Stephan James, who plays Carl Weathers. We were beating the crap out of each other and figuring out how to box. I had gained a bunch of weight, and I was trying to actually cut a few pounds, so I was in those sweatsuits, like a garbage-bag type thing. On the way to the gym, I would listen to Stallone and on the way home.… Everything I could find up to 1980, 1985, every piece of Stallone footage that existed.

I [asked] Seth Rogen, “Dude, how do you handle this stuff?” And he said, “Just go with the flow.” It was such a simple answer, but from somebody like him, I was like, He’s got a good grip on this. The simplicity of it landed.

Philip Seymour Hoffman is one. Chadwick Boseman. Christian Bale, Heath Ledger.

[The first Rocky] is the best movie—but when I was younger, the one that caught my eye was four. Rocky IV is nuts. —F.T.

Jacket by Versace. Shirt by 73London. Pants by Umit Benan. Earring (throughout), his own.

(from l.) On Ambrossi: All clothing by Gucci. Shoes by Christian Louboutin. Pocket square by Brioni. Sunglasses by Ahlem. On Calvo: Jacket, pants, and boots by Tom Ford. Scarf, stylist’s own. Sunglasses by Jacques Marie Mage.

(from l.) On Ambrossi: Jacket and pants by Chanel. Shirt by Factor’s. Shoes by Marsèll. Pin by Cartier. On Calvo: All clothing, tie, and shoes by Ralph Lauren Purple Label. Watch by Cartier.

Ages: Ambrossi, 42 | Calvo, 35Breakout moment: Cowriting and directing La Bola Negra, the gay Spanish historical epic loosely based on an unfinished Federico García Lorca play.——————————————

Javier Ambrossi: Very important. We understood that sometimes people expect LGBTQ+ stories to be niche or for a specific audience. We wanted to do a queer story about universal love.

Ambrossi: It’s a way to put in context how different we are. We change a lot, and the story of our grandparents and our story is very different.

Javier Calvo: What do we do with the freedom our ancestors fought for, and died for?

Calvo: Isabelle Huppert. For me, she’s everything.

Ambrossi: I will go with Julia Roberts. My Best Friend’s Wedding is a very important queer story. The relationship between a woman and a gay man—it was the first time I saw that onscreen. And Rupert Everett was so bold, and I could tell in his eyes that he was gay. I was a kid and I was like, “He’s not faking it.”

How did you celebrate when you won best director at Cannes?

Ambrossi: I put the award on the table and went to sleep. And then Javi came over at 8 a.m.…

Ambrossi: “Give me the award!” And he took it! —A.P.

(from l.) On Ippolito: Sunglasses by Jacques Marie Mage. Necklace by Cartier. On Chike: Shirt and pants by Brioni. Sunglasses by Tom Ford. On Thiele: Jacket by McQueen. Shirt by Factor’s. Pants by Versace.

#6746. Cut It Out! Hollywood’s Red Carpets Are Finding New Ways to Show Skin

Kim Kardashian has never met a cutout she didn’t like. The reality star and fashion provocateur has made something of a signature out of showing skin in unexpected places—she loves an exposed hip, a plunging neckline, and a dress that appears to defy the laws of physics. At last night’s 2026 LACMA Art+Film Gala in Los Angeles, she was in familiar territory, wearing a burgundy sequined Gucci gown by Demna that was all business from the front, with its high neck, long sleeves, and sculpted silhouette, and decidedly less so from the side. A dramatic slash across the waist revealed an expanse of skin above the hip.

And she was far from alone. If the evening’s red carpet was anything to go by, Hollywood’s appetite for the naked dress has evolved into something more architectural and off-beat. Forget the romantically diaphanous or the all-out sheer, the latest approach to showing skin is all about strategic exposure. Think a dramatically placed opening, a vertiginous slit, and plunging, crack-skimming backs. Sometimes, what a dress conceals is just as important as what it reveals.

Leading the charge, of course, was the cohort of celebrities dressed by Gucci, where Demna has established a provocative, high-octane strain of glamour. Rosie Huntington-Whiteley wore a black, long-sleeved custom gown with exaggerated shoulders and a severe, almost monastic front that gave way to a completely exposed back and butt, with a daring slit extending to the hip, fastened with a small jeweled detail. Restrained from one angle, outrageously risqué from another.

Fellow model Amber Valletta also opted for custom Gucci, in a black column gown with a plunging open back, a silver ornamental detail, and a thigh-baring slit that extended almost to her waist. Emily Ratajkowski chose a white draped Gucci number with a plunging neckline and dramatically open sides, paired with a sky-high leg slit.

There were plenty more variations on the theme. Alix Earle embraced the evening’s maximalist mood in a silver Gucci, disco-ready halter gown dripping with strands of shimmering embellishment, with a thigh-high slit emerging from beneath the metallic fringe. Olympic skier Lindsey Vonn also turned to Gucci, wearing a glittering, one-shouldered purple gown with an asymmetrical neckline and a dramatic slit that revealed a sheer black-stockinged leg. Candice Swanepoel took a similarly sparkling approach in a silver, crystal-strewn gown with a plunging neckline and two daringly high slits, with more sparkle cascading over her legs.

Not everyone was in Gucci, though. Madelaine Petsch opted for a look from Georges Hobeika’s spring 2027 collection, with a black halter-neck bodice that offered a hint of side-boob, and which plunged almost to the waist before meeting a cream floral-embroidered pencil skirt.

The naked dress has long been a Hollywood fixture. Body-conscious designs are beloved by the Kardashian-Jenner clan, having a deep understanding of the impact of a well-placed flash of flesh. But then there’s people like Anya Taylor-Joy, a champion of the sensuous and barely there, keeping a more ghostly and romantic bent with winter-white corsetry by Dilara Findikoglu and forays into vampy Tom Ford. This new iteration, however, uses precision cuts and dramatic contrasts to draw the eye to particular parts of the body.

With Demna’s Gucci helping to usher in a new mood of all-out, unabashed glamour, it seems the red carpet is entering its next undressed era.
